claims.text: The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and form a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Greater atomic-scale uniformity suppresses thermodynamically driven phase segregation at high operating temperatures.
Suppressing phase segregation maintains both structural and chemical stability across catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
Slow annealing followed by controlled cooling enhances local atomic-mixing uniformity.
Rapid quenching induces local chemical heterogeneities.
Highly uniform atomic distributions balance the competing mixing enthalpies among constituent elements.
Balanced mixing enthalpies minimize local energy gradients.
Minimized local energy gradients delay the onset of phase segregation.
Local elemental enrichment or depletion creates regions with increased driving forces for phase separation.
Local enrichment or depletion produces lattice distortions that trigger structural degradation at high temperatures.
Slow-annealed, controlled-cooled nanoparticles will show less secondary-phase formation than rapidly quenched nanoparticles over 473–1923 K.
Slow-annealed, controlled-cooled nanoparticles will retain catalytic and thermoelectric performance across 473–1923 K.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit measurable phase segregation across the tested temperature range.
Phase segregation in rapidly quenched nanoparticles will be accompanied by catalytic and thermoelectric performance degradation.
The predicted behavior is limited to alloy constituents whose mixing enthalpies do not overwhelmingly favor segregation.
Large intrinsic mixing-enthalpy differences can destabilize even uniformly processed nanoparticles at the highest tested temperatures.
